problem: Sim2real for legged-robot visual navigation is assumed to require higher-fidelity physics simulation, but dynamic simulation is slow (limiting RL scale) and policies overfit to simulator physics and to imperfect low-level controllers that cannot be modeled for black-box robots like Spot.
motivation: Reducing the sim2real gap is a central challenge for training robots in simulation. For tasks with abstract action spaces such as navigation, the low-level physics may be unnecessary, and simulation speed may matter more than fidelity. The authors run a large controlled study (2 simulators, 3 robots, kinematic vs dynamic) to test this.
key_idea: Train the high-level visual navigation policy in fast kinematic (teleport) simulation and delegate low-level motion to the robot's own black-box controller on hardware, optionally adding a small real-data actuation noise model.
insight: Kinematic-trained policies beat dynamic-trained ones even when evaluated under dynamic control (e.g. A1 62.1% vs 24.2% SR in iGibson Dynamic), and they transfer across simulators and controllers, while dynamic policies drop sharply across simulators (A1 49.8% in Habitat-Dynamic vs 22.3% in iGibson-Dynamic). The reason is largely scale: kinematic training gets ~10x more experience (500M vs 50M steps) in 2.3x less wall-clock time, and dynamic policies also overfit to simulator physics (the overfitting gap grows with training in Table 3). Real-world results confirm this: kinematic policies reach 100% SR vs 40-67% for dynamic.
method: Hierarchical policy: a high-level policy outputs CoM velocities (Vx, Vy, ω) at 1 Hz; the low-level controller is simulated (dynamic) or abstracted away (kinematic)
High-level network: ResNet-18 depth encoder + 2-layer LSTM with a Gaussian action head, trained with DD-PPO (8 GPUs x 8 envs, lr 2.5e-4, gamma 0.99)
Kinematic simulation: Euler-integrate the commanded velocity and teleport the robot; the robot stays in place if the new pose would collide
Dynamic simulation: Bullet at 240 Hz with a Raibert controller for training and an MPC controller for evaluation, as a proxy for unknown real controllers
Reward: geodesic progress, collision -0.03, fall -5, success +10, slack -0.002, plus a new backward-motion penalty -0.03
Actuation noise model: fit a diagonal Gaussian to 6,000 real Spot samples (decoupled or coupled) and add it to commanded velocities during kinematic training
Zero-shot deployment on Spot: send the policy velocities directly to the Boston Dynamics controller, with a depth camera and egomotion sensing

setting.backbone: ResNet-18 + 2-layer LSTM policy (trained from scratch with DD-PPO)
setting.training_data: RL in HM3D + Gibson scenes (~1000 scans), 3 days on 8 GPUs per policy (kinematic ~500M steps, dynamic ~50M steps); 6,000 real Spot actuation-noise samples for the noise variants
setting.observation: egocentric depth + goal relative to the robot (egomotion / GPS+compass)
setting.action_space: continuous CoM velocities (Vx, Vy, ω) at 1 Hz, converted to joint torques by a low-level controller
setting.privileged: none (a real-world Spot's egomotion estimates are used for the goal and for success measurement)

numbers.eval_set_note: 5 episodes x 3 seeds = 15 real-world episodes in the LAB environment (avg ~10 m)
numbers.extra: zero-shot sim2real on Spot; BD black-box controller
trained with actuation noise from 6,000 real Spot samples

The last entry's Table-1 sim numbers come from the LAB scan in simulation, not the val split, so treat its split label with caution.
results: Kinematic-trained policies reach 100% real-world SR and 82-89% SPL on Spot, while dynamic-trained ones reach only 40.0% (Habitat) and 67.7% (iGibson) SR, with many more collisions (41.2 vs 3.1). In simulation, kinematic policies beat dynamic ones even under dynamic evaluation (+12% SR for A1 with 2.3x less wall-clock), and actuation noise modeling raises SPL by 4.6-5.6 points.
limitations: Assumes a robust black-box low-level controller exists on the hardware; only applies to tasks with abstract action spaces (navigation, pick/place), not dexterous manipulation or locomotion
Real-world evaluation is small (15 episodes, one environment, one robot), and actuation noise is a simple Gaussian model
builds_on: Learning navigation skills for legged robots with learned robot embeddings
